posts.title: Five morning habits for steadier blood sugar
posts.author: Dr. Ritam Roy
posts.summary: How you spend the first hour of the day shapes your sugar for the next twelve. Five simple habits that help.
posts.body:
Most of my patients ask about *what* to eat. Fewer ask about *when* and *how* — yet the first hour of the morning sets the tone for the whole day.

## 1. Check, don't guess
If you use a glucometer, test your **fasting sugar** a few days a week before tea or breakfast. Write it down. A log of real numbers helps me adjust your medicines far more safely than a single reading at the chamber.

## 2. Take medicines at a fixed time
Metformin, insulin and other medicines work best on a routine. Keep them next to your toothbrush or tea cups so you never miss them.

## 3. Walk before the day gets busy
Even **15–20 minutes of brisk walking** improves how your body handles sugar for hours afterwards. A walk after dinner helps too.

## 4. Build a balanced breakfast
Instead of only *muri*, white bread or biscuits, add protein and fibre:
- a boiled egg or a bowl of dal-chilla
- sprouts or a small bowl of curd
- a whole fruit (guava, apple, orange) rather than juice

## 5. Go easy on sugar in tea
Cut it by half this week and by half again next week. Your taste adjusts within a fortnight.

> Small changes, done every day, beat big changes done for a week.

If your fasting sugar stays above **130 mg/dL** on most days, please book a review — your treatment may need fine-tuning.

posts.title: Are you taking your thyroid tablet the right way?
posts.author: Dr. Ritam Roy
posts.summary: Levothyroxine is one of the simplest medicines to take — and one of the easiest to take wrongly.
posts.body:
Many patients with hypothyroidism keep getting abnormal TSH reports even though they "never miss a tablet". Very often the problem is *how* the tablet is taken.

## The basics
- Take it **first thing in the morning on an empty stomach**, with plain water.
- Wait **30–60 minutes** before tea, coffee or breakfast.
- Keep **calcium, iron and antacid** tablets at least **4 hours** apart.

## When to recheck TSH
After any dose change, test TSH after **6–8 weeks**. Once stable, a yearly test is usually enough — unless you are pregnant or planning pregnancy, when it needs closer monitoring.

## Never stop on your own
Feeling better is a sign the tablet is working, not that you no longer need it. Always discuss before changing the dose.

Bring your last two thyroid reports to your next visit.

posts.title: Diabetes and your kidneys: two tests that matter
posts.author: Dr. Ritam Roy
posts.summary: Kidney damage from diabetes is silent for years. Two inexpensive tests catch it early.
posts.body:
Diabetic kidney disease causes **no symptoms** in its early stages. By the time swelling of the feet or breathlessness appears, much damage is already done. The good news: two simple tests can pick it up years earlier.

## 1. Urine ACR (albumin-creatinine ratio)
A spot urine test that detects tiny amounts of protein leaking through the kidneys. An ACR above **30 mg/g** on repeat testing is an early warning sign.

## 2. Serum creatinine with eGFR
A blood test that estimates how well your kidneys filter. Your report will show an **eGFR** value; below 60 needs attention.

## How often?
Everyone with diabetes should do both tests **at least once a year** — more often if they are abnormal or if you also have high blood pressure.

## What protects the kidneys
- Good sugar control (HbA1c target agreed with your doctor)
- Blood pressure below **130/80** for most patients
- Avoiding painkillers like diclofenac and ibuprofen without advice
- Not smoking

Several modern diabetes medicines also protect the kidneys. Ask me whether they suit you.
